# 普曜經

**ID:** T0186

**Category:** 本緣部類
**Original Category:** 本緣部
**Byline:** 西晉 竺法護譯
**Dynasty:** 西晉
**Date:** 308
**Juans:** 8

## Contributors
- 竺法護 (A000749)

## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

The earliest complete Chinese translation of the *Lalitavistara* — the celebrated Mahāyāna Buddha-biography in mixed prose and verse, recounting the descent, birth, youth, renunciation, and awakening of Śākyamuni in *līlā*-mode (the Buddha's life as cosmic play). Translated by [竺法護](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%AB%BA%E6%B3%95%E8%AD%B7) Dharmarakṣa in the Western Jìn. Signature: 「西晉月氏三藏竺法護譯」. The Taishō header notes the alternative title 方等本起 ("Origin-of-the-Vaipulya") and cross-references [T187](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0043), the later Tang re-translation by [地婆訶羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%B0%E5%A9%86%E8%A8%B6%E7%BE%85) Divākara.

**Abstract**

T186 is the principal Western-Jìn translation of the Mahāyāna *Lalitavistara* tradition; the *Chū sānzàng jì jí* 出三藏記集 ([KR6s0084](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6s/KR6s0084)) records its translation date as Yǒngjiā 永嘉 2 = 308 CE at Tiānshuǐ 天水. The Indic source corresponds closely to the Sanskrit *Lalitavistara* edited by Lefmann (1902–1908) and Vaidya (1958), though T186 reflects an earlier and slightly different Sanskrit recension than the Tang re-translation T187 ([地婆訶羅](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%9C%B0%E5%A9%86%E8%A8%B6%E7%BE%85) Divākara, c. 685 CE). The two Chinese versions of the *Lalitavistara* — separated by some 380 years — have been one of the principal test-cases in the comparative study of Chinese Buddhist translation idiom.

T186 is doctrinally consequential as the principal Mahāyāna Buddha-biography in Chinese during the period from Western Jìn through the early-medieval period, before Aśvaghoṣa's *Buddhacarita* came into wider circulation through [曇無讖](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%9B%87%E7%84%A1%E8%AE%96) Dharmakṣema's *[Fó suǒxíng zàn (T192)](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6b/KR6b0049)*. The *Lalitavistara*'s emphasis on the Buddha's life as cosmic *līlā* — and on the Mahāyāna proposition that the Buddha's apparent biography is a soteriological *upāya* — was foundational for East-Asian Buddhist Buddha-biography reception.
